description: Conversational learning cards with subtitle, body paragraphs, and takeaway per card.

article.title: Grit Is Overrated: When Persistence Becomes Self-Sabotage
article.author: Dr. Marcus Stone

cards.title: Grit Keeps You in the Wrong Career
cards.subtitle: Persistence can be a strength—and also why you're still miserable after eight years.
body: Grit is celebrated. But persistence in the wrong direction is just slow failure. Sometimes the braver move is to quit.
Knowing when to stop is as valuable as knowing when to push. Persistence without direction can turn into sunk cost fallacy.
Quitting isn't always weakness; it can be strategic.
cards.takeaway: Grit in the wrong direction can be costly; sometimes quitting is the right call.

cards.title: Growth Mindset Ignores Structural Barriers
cards.subtitle: Effort matters, but so do resources, connections, and systemic advantages.
body: Growth mindset says ability is malleable through effort. That's partly true. But effort alone doesn't determine outcomes.
Your competitor might have capital, connections, and credentials. Mindset is necessary, not sufficient.
Ignoring structural barriers can make it seem like individuals are solely responsible for outcomes—which isn't fair or accurate.
cards.takeaway: Effort matters, but structural factors constrain what effort can achieve.

cards.title: Positive Thinking Doesn't Outperform Realistic Planning
cards.subtitle: Visualizing success feels good; planning for obstacles actually helps.
body: Positive visualization is motivating, but it doesn't prepare you for what goes wrong. Mental contrasting—imagining success and obstacles—tends to outperform pure optimism.
Obstacles need strategies, not just affirmations. Realism beats fantasy when it comes to execution.
Optimism can motivate; planning is what gets you there.
cards.takeaway: Combine positive vision with realistic planning for obstacles.

cards.title: Morning Routines Are Survivorship Bias
cards.subtitle: Successful people wake at 5am—but so do plenty of people who aren't successful.
body: CEOs share their routines. You rarely hear from the people who wake at 5am and still struggle. We're copying a correlation, not a cause.
Success stories are selected samples. The routine might not have caused success; success might have made the routine notable.
Mimicking habits doesn't automatically transfer context.
cards.takeaway: Success routines are often survivorship bias; copy with caution.

cards.title: Goals Create Binary Failure Conditions
cards.subtitle: You lost fifteen pounds but wanted twenty—and it feels like failure.
body: Goals create pass/fail judgments. Progress that doesn't hit the target can feel like failure, even when you've made real improvement.
Systems—ongoing habits—produce continuous improvement without arbitrary endpoints.
Missed goals can discourage; good systems tend to compound.
cards.takeaway: Systems often serve you better than all-or-nothing goals.

cards.title: Self-Help Advice Is Context-Dependent
cards.subtitle: 'Be assertive' helps the timid person; it can make the aggressive person worse.
body: Self-help often assumes universal applicability. But people start from different baselines. The same advice can help one person and harm another.
Know your starting point. Your problem might be the opposite of what the advice assumes.
One size fits none; tailor advice to where you actually are.
cards.takeaway: Advice depends on context; apply it to your specific situation.

cards.title: Productivity Porn Feels Like Progress
cards.subtitle: You spent three hours optimizing your task manager and completed zero tasks.
body: Reading about productivity, tweaking systems, and planning workflows can feel productive. Often they're procrastination in disguise.
Meta-work isn't real work. Optimization can be a form of avoidance.
Executing usually beats planning. At some point, you have to do the thing.
cards.takeaway: Optimization can be avoidance; execution matters more.

cards.title: Failure Is Only a Teacher If You Reflect
cards.subtitle: You failed, moved on, and learned nothing. Reflection is what turns failure into data.
body: Failure doesn't automatically teach. Most people fail, feel bad, and repeat the same mistakes.
Learning requires deliberately extracting lessons. What went wrong? What would you do differently?
Experience without reflection is often just repetition.
cards.takeaway: Reflection converts failure into useful information.

cards.title: Habits Form Through Repetition, Not Motivation
cards.subtitle: Waiting to feel motivated often means waiting forever. Action usually comes first.
body: Motivation is unreliable. Discipline—doing it regardless of how you feel—builds habits. Once the habit forms, it runs without much motivation.
Waiting for motivation can delay indefinitely. Action often precedes motivation, not the reverse.
Habits automate behavior and reduce reliance on willpower.
cards.takeaway: Don't wait for motivation; start small and let repetition build the habit.

cards.title: Identity Change Beats Behavior Change
cards.subtitle: 'I am a runner' tends to work better than 'I will run three times a week.'
body: Behavior goals are external. Identity goals are internal. Runners run. People trying to run often don't.
Identity shifts can create automatic behavior alignment. Becoming someone is sometimes easier than forcing yourself to do something.
The framing matters. Who you're becoming can drive what you do.
cards.takeaway: Identity-based goals often sustain behavior better than behavior-based ones.

cards.title: Environment Shapes Behavior More Than Willpower
cards.subtitle: Cookies on the counter beat willpower most of the time.
body: Behavior tends to follow the path of least resistance. Changing your environment is often more effective than relying on self-control.
Willpower is finite. Proximity and convenience shape what we do.
Design the space, not just the effort. Make the desired behavior easier and the undesired one harder.
cards.takeaway: Environment design often beats personal discipline.

cards.title: Rest Is Productive, Not Indulgent
cards.subtitle: Working through the weekend can leave you sluggish Monday; a day off might have produced more.
body: Recovery enables performance. Chronic work without rest tends to reduce quality over time.
Rest isn't laziness—it's strategic restoration. Fatigue decreases output.
Marathons require pacing, not constant sprints.
cards.takeaway: Rest compounds future performance; it's not indulgence.

cards.title: Comparison Is Inevitable, Not Evil
cards.subtitle: 'Don't compare yourself' is unrealistic; comparison is hardwired. The trick is how you use it.
body: Social comparison provides feedback and motivation. The problem isn't comparison itself—it's upward comparison without learning.
Compare to improve, not to despair. Use it strategically.
Eliminating comparison isn't the goal; managing it is.
cards.takeaway: Comparison is information; use it to learn, not to spiral.

cards.title: Peak Experiences Don't Sustain Change
cards.subtitle: The seminar was transformative; two weeks later you're back to old patterns.
body: Intense experiences create temporary motivation. The high fades. Lasting change usually requires systems and repetition.
Peak moments can inspire; routines sustain. The seminar might be a spark, but it's not the fire.
If you want change to stick, build structure around it.
cards.takeaway: Peak experiences inspire; systems and repetition sustain change.
